source.title: Emergent Capabilities Arise Randomly from Learning Sparse Attention Patterns
source.authors: Vatsal Baherwani; Zixi Chen; Shi-Kai Qiu; Andrew Gordon Wilson; Pavel Izmailov

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different causal head-patching analysis to test whether attention patterns contribute to indirect object identification, rather than testing the original GPT-2 small circuit and its criteria.
record.gate_note: The IOI patching and head-pattern findings bear on V1; the reported dependence on the number of patched heads bears on V5. The paper does not test the complete 26-head, 7-class circuit or its faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria. Its reported pre-pretraining effects on IOI are recorded as related findings, not as evidence about a circuit version. Cited results about the original IOI circuit and results on synthetic tasks are not counted as this study's results on the claim.
record.test_reason: The study tracks IOI emergence across Pythia training checkpoints and seeds. Its only result bearing on a claim version is qualitative: one selected head in a Pythia checkpoint becomes name-mover-like when IOI emerges. That bears weakly on V3, the same head roles in another model family and across checkpoints. It does not study GPT-2 small, so it cannot bear on V1. Its top-K patching is the study's own selection method, not an evaluation of the IOI circuit, so it does not bear on V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that capabilities, including IOI, emerge abruptly and at random points in training when task-relevant attention patterns are learned across several heads. They also conclude that patching those patterns into the earlier checkpoint elicits the capability early. For IOI they describe one selected head as roughly name-mover-like and note that IOI is often absent in most seeds at about 124M scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study tracks emergence across training checkpoints and patches post-emergence attention patterns into pre-emergence checkpoints, selecting heads by their effect on correct-token probability. It does not reproduce the original study's full circuit analysis or stated evaluation criteria.
record.method_sensitivity: For the patching analysis, the increase in target-token probability grows with K, the number of selected causal heads patched.

fits_no_version.finding: Patching post-emergence attention patterns of the top-K causal heads into the pre-emergence checkpoint elicits the correct IOI token. Larger K gives a larger probability increase, which the authors read as the capability being distributed across heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For IOI in Pythia, the capability is bottlenecked by attention patterns learned jointly across multiple heads.

fits_no_version.finding: In one seed, NCA pre-pretraining led to IOI emerging within 5,000 C4 steps; scratch and Dyck training did not. This is preliminary, based on four seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Synthetic pre-pretraining may affect whether IOI emerges during training.

record.problems: The IOI circuit evidence is qualitative: exact patching values, checkpoint, seed, and head identity are not stated. The paper visualizes one IOI head and does not test the full circuit or its faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Its pre-pretraining results use only four random seeds, which the authors say limits statistical power.
record.rows_left_out: Synthetic-task results and other capability results were left out because they do not test the IOI circuit claim. Cited findings about the original IOI circuit were excluded because they are not results from this study.

untested.parts: The study does not examine GPT-2 small at all, nor the 26-head, 7-class circuit or its criteria.
There is no name-mover ablation and no test of backup heads.

The study does not identify duplicate-token, S-inhibition, induction or backup heads in Pythia. It does not compare across sizes with head identities, and it does not test component reuse for other tasks.
There is no comparison of circuit-finding methods.
It does not evaluate the IOI circuit's faithfulness or completeness under different ablations, metrics or prompt distributions.
Only the single canonical John/Mary prompt is used.

missing.what: For IOI, the authors say the capability is often absent in most Pythia seeds even at GPT-2-small scale. This bears on how reliably IOI and its circuit arise in comparable models; no row records it.
Figure 2(a) shows IOI emergence step against Pythia model scale (14M–410M, ten seeds). The values are figure-only, and no row records this result.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the rows to V1 and V5. Those links are wrong: the model is Pythia, not GPT-2 small, and the K-dependence reflects the study's own patching selection, not sensitivity of the IOI circuit's evaluation. The only defensible link is R2 to V3, and it is weak: one qualitative head on one prompt, with an unstated model size and seed. The paper cites Wang et al. only as the source of the prompt and for comparing the head's role.

versions.untested_parts: The complete 26-head, 7-class circuit; the stated roles of all head classes; and the faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria are not evaluated.
The study does not ablate main name-mover heads and test whether backup heads take over.
It does not establish that the same circuit is present across models, sizes, or checkpoints, or that its components are reused for other tasks.
It does not compare circuit-finding methods, ablation types, or evaluation metrics for recovery of the same circuit.

It reports dependence on the number of patched heads, but does not compare ablation types or metrics, assess prompt-distribution sensitivity for IOI, or measure the original circuit's faithfulness and completeness.
The IOI analysis uses the illustrated example; it does not test other name orders, templates, or prompts with more names.

illustrated IOI example; other prompts not stated

rows.measure: Change in probability of the correct next token
rows.baseline: Pre-emergence model without the attention-pattern patch; numerical value not stated
rows.value: Figure only; the text says patching causal heads can elicit emergence in the earlier checkpoint and that higher K produces a stronger increase in target-token probability.
rows.note: The method selects top causal heads using individual-head effects; the text does not report the IOI curve's numerical values or identify the exact checkpoint or seed.
rows.check: The subject is Pythia, not GPT-2 small, so V1 does not apply. V5 concerns how the IOI circuit's faithfulness and completeness depend on the ablation or metric. This row instead reports the effect of the study's own top-K head-patching selection, and the Figure 2(d) statement about K is a generic caption covering all tasks. The heads are not identified as IOI circuit classes, and no IOI numbers are given. It is the study's own method, not a test of the circuit.

rows.subject: Pythia model (specific checkpoint not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Inspect the attention pattern of one selected head around IOI emergence.

conditions.value: one selected attention head; layer and head index not stated

rows.measure: Attention weights from the last query token to the names
rows.value: Before emergence the last query attends substantially to John; after emergence attention shifts mostly to Mary. The authors describe the head as roughly corresponding to name-mover behavior.
rows.note: The paper describes the plotted pattern qualitatively. It says this is at the scale of GPT-2-small (124M), but does not identify the particular Pythia checkpoint in the IOI result.
rows.check: This row bears on V3 (another model and training checkpoints), not V1, which is specific to GPT-2 small. The authors describe the head as only 'roughly' name-mover-like. It is a single selected head on one prompt, with the layer, head index, model size and seed unstated. No other head classes are identified, so the 'same circuit' is shown only very partially.
